\title{Measuring Complex Tastes: A Multiple Factor Analysis of Preferences, Consumption, and Evaluations in Musical Taste}

\author{Omar Lizardo\\ \small University of California, Los Angeles} \date{October 2026}

\begin{document}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
\noindent This paper develops a way to measure complex tastes---cases where what people like, do, and praise do not line up---using data that record preferences, engagement, and evaluations of the same objects, whether genre categories or specific cultural items. The approach applies Multiple Factor Analysis (MFA), a Geometric Data Analysis (GDA) method, and lets us ask concrete questions about complex tastes: Do preference, engagement, and evaluation contribute equally to the structure that emerges? Do some dimensions of complex taste hang together more than others? The method also captures a duality: individuals vary in how much their own tastes are complex, and genres vary in how much they attract complex tastes from the people who encounter them. I demonstrate the approach using data on Americans' tastes in twenty musical genres, collected around 2012.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Sociologists have measured cultural taste in at least three different ways \citep{ma2026tastes}. One tradition treats taste as \emph{preference}: a person's affective response to a cultural object. A second treats it as an orientation toward \emph{consumption}: actual participation or engagement in a cultural field. A third treats it as a faculty expressed in \emph{valuation}: judgments about the quality or status of cultural objects. Rather than resolving this ambiguity by fiat, \citet{ma2026tastes} argues that taste should be understood pluralistically, as a person's ``thick subjectivity'' in a cultural field---a multidimensional orientation expressed through the multiple aspects of action that guide our preferences, engagement, and evaluations.

Taking taste's multiple aspects seriously sharpens the idea of \emph{complex taste}. In simple tastes, the aspects agree: what a person likes, does, and values all point the same way. In complex tastes they do not: the guilty pleasure (liked and consumed but not valued), the taste pose (liked and valued but not consumed), distanced consumption (consumed but neither liked nor valued), and their kin \citep{ma2026tastes}.

This paper takes that pluralist conception seriously and builds a measurement strategy to match. The strategy applies Multiple Factor Analysis (MFA) \citep{pages2014mfa,abdi2013mfa}---a member of the Geometric Data Analysis (GDA) family that \citet{bourdieu1984distinction} used in his classic study \citep{rouanet2000geometric-a44, roux2004geometric-65c}---to a data structure in which each cultural object is described by three sets of indicators, one per each aspect of complex taste. MFA's block structure lets us ask the questions the theory of complex tastes raises directly, such as how strong are the links between preference, consumption, and evaluation? Do the three aspects contribute equally to the shared structure of taste? And what does the geometric signature of independent taste aspects look like when mapped to the same shared space?

\section{Data and Measures}

\subsection{Data Source}

This analysis uses the Survey Sample International (SSI) 2012 Cultural Tastes Survey \citep{lizardo2012ssi},\footnote{The survey data and documentation are publicly available at \url{https://olizardo.github.io/SSI-2012/}.} a nationally representative sample of $N = 2{,}276$ U.S. adults surveyed in 2012. The survey asked respondents about their relationship to twenty musical genres, capturing how they feel about each genre, whether they engage with it, and how they perceive the people who enjoy it. After removing the 17 respondents with incomplete data on any of the 60 analysis variables, the working sample contains $N = 2{,}259$ respondents.

\subsection{Operationalizing the Three Aspects of Taste}

To measure complex tastes, we need distinct measures of preference, consumption, and evaluation for each genre. The operationalization is straightforward, built on three survey questions.

\emph{Preference} captures affective response. Respondents rated each genre on a four-point scale: like, dislike, neither like nor dislike, or not familiar. I code preference as binary: a genre is coded $1$ if the respondent likes it, and $0$ otherwise. This coding includes unfamiliar genres as non-preferences, on the reasoning that genuine affective preference requires at least knowing the object. If you've never heard of a genre, you haven't preferred it.

\emph{Consumption} measures engagement. The survey asked respondents whether they had listened to each genre in the past month, a straightforward behavioral indicator. Consumption is coded $1$ if the respondent checked having listened, and $0$ otherwise.

\emph{Evaluation} is the trickiest to operationalize because status attributions are not simple binaries. The survey presented respondents with a check-all-that-apply list of social characteristics typically attributed to each genre's fans (college-educated, middle-class, upper-class, working-class, lower-class, etc.). The problem is that responses are often contradictory: a respondent might check both ``college-educated'' and ``not college-educated,'' or indicate both ``middle-class'' and ``upper-class.'' These contradictions reflect genuine social ambiguity (some genres do attract mixed-status audiences), but for our purposes, we need a single measure of whether respondents attribute high status to a genre's typical fans.

The solution is to code high evaluation only when the respondent signals \emph{unambiguous} high status: either they checked college-educated without also checking not college-educated, \emph{or} they checked middle or upper class without also checking working or lower class. This conservative standard requires that the respondent not contradict themselves. A genre is coded $1$ on evaluation if at least one of these unambiguous high-status signals is present, and $0$ otherwise. This coding reflects a genuine judgment call: respondents grant unambiguous high status to a genre's fans less often than they like the genre or listen to it.

Table~\ref{tab:genre-rates} shows the prevalence of each coding. Overall, $41.7\%$ of genre-responses are coded $1$ on preference, $22.9\%$ on consumption, and $20.7\%$ on evaluation. The step down from preference to evaluation is striking: respondents like more genres than they listen to, and listen to more than they credit with high status. The unambiguous-status standard is demanding, requiring clear social positioning without internal contradiction, so evaluation becomes the least frequently affirmed aspect of taste.

\section{Analytic Strategy}

Our data gives us three separate pictures of each person's taste: what they like, what they listen to, and what they think about the people who do. These three pictures might overlap heavily (a person who likes opera probably listens to it and sees its fans as high status), or they might diverge sharply (someone might listen to hip-hop while considering it low status). We need a method that asks: How much do these three pictures agree? Do they contribute equally to a single coherent picture of musical taste? And where, geometrically, do people end up when their three pictures don't line up?

Multiple Factor Analysis (MFA) \citep{pages2014mfa,abdi2013mfa} is built precisely for this kind of problem. It takes data organized into distinct blocks of variables---here, the three aspects of taste---and builds a single shared picture of the people while making sure no one block dominates. The MFA literature calls these variable sets ``groups''; we use \emph{blocks of variables}, or \emph{aspects} when referring specifically to preference, engagement, and evaluation, reserving ``group'' for its ordinary sociological meaning. In the geometric data analysis tradition, the distinct values a variable can take (here, yes/no) are called \emph{modalities}; here, we use \textit{categories}. The MFA approach proceeds in two steps, which we describe in the following sections. 

\subsection{Constructing the Global Complex Taste Space}

The raw data is a table with one row per respondent and sixty columns: twenty genres, each measured on three aspects. Each entry is binary, containing a 1 if the person likes/listens to/evaluates the genre highly, and 0 otherwise. 

In the first step, we run a separate analysis on just the liking data (20 genres, 2,259 respondents), treating it as a two-way table of yes/no responses. This analysis shows how respondents cluster by what they like. We repeat the process independently for listening and for evaluations. In technical terms, each of these is a Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA) on one block of twenty binary variables and the same number of individuals. The result of each separate MCA is a map of the respondents, showing who is similar to whom in terms of liking alone, listening alone, or evaluations alone.

After the first step, the next step is to merge these three separate pictures into one. But we face a problem here because if one aspect naturally has stronger patterns than another (if listening, say, reveals much sharper clustering than evaluations), it will dominate the combined picture. To prevent this, we weight each aspect inversely to the magnitude of the first dimension's eigenvalue on the separate MCA we just described. The first dimension of the MCA for preference had an eigenvalue of $0.155$; for consumption, $0.127$; for evaluation, $0.194$. The aspect with the largest eigenvalue ($\lambda_1$) has the strongest patterns, so we downweight it by using the weight $1/\lambda_1$. That gives weights of $6.45$ for preference ($1/0.155$), $7.90$ for consumption ($1/0.127$), and $5.15$ for evaluation ($1/0.194$).\footnote{Respondents who give a constant answer within an aspect---liking all twenty genres or none, listening to all or none, granting unambiguous high status to the fans of all twenty genres or of none ($N = 412$, mostly the $321$ who grant status to no genre)---are treated as supplementary individuals, projected onto the space rather than contributing to its construction. They are excluded from the active subsample ($N = 1{,}847$) because constancy within a block is a nonresponse pattern, not a substantive taste position; respondents constant in one block typically vary in others. As a robustness check (script 11), we re-estimated the MFA treating them as active and the previous fit as supplementary. The RV structure is preserved ($0.35$, $0.01$, $0.02$). The first two dimensions recover their counterparts ($r = 0.87$ and $0.89$) but exchange rank order. The status-valuation dimension (now dimension 4) recovers its old counterpart ($r = 0.95$) but is displaced by an additional preference-and-consumption axis (new dimension 3). The substance of the four interpreted dimensions thus survives this choice, though the placement of the status axis does not.} We apply these weights by multiplying each entry in each aspect-specific data table by its corresponding weight before combining them into the global analysis. The intuition is like handicapping in golf: the aspect with the strongest internal structure gets downweighted so all three contribute equally to the final picture. The result is the ``complex taste space''---a single map of respondents where all three aspects are heard equally.\footnote{As a robustness check, we re-estimated the same MFA with each block analyzed by scaled PCA instead of MCA; the results hold. Eigenvalues, RV coefficients, and individual coordinates correlate at $r > 0.96$ across the first four dimensions. The main difference is how rare categories are weighted: MCA emphasizes rare (distinctive) answers, a feature we want here since unusual taste patterns carry theoretical interest.}

\subsubsection{Independence or Redundancy of Aspects of Complex Tastes}

Before we interpret the combined space, we need to answer a basic question: \emph{Are the three aspects empirically separate, or are they measuring the same thing from different angles?} If they're really just capturing one underlying dimension, preference alone would suffice. But if they're genuinely independent, then complex tastes become possible---people can occupy completely different positions when you rank them by what they like versus what they listen to versus what they value.

The RV coefficient answers this question. It measures how similarly two aspects rank respondents relative to each other. RV ranges from 0 (complete independence: knowing someone likes many genres tells you nothing about how much they listen) to 1 (perfect alignment: whoever likes most also listens most and values most). It's the multivariate cousin of a correlation coefficient, comparing not single variables but entire blocks.\footnote{Formally, for each aspect $h$, the configuration matrix $\mathbf{S}_h$ captures pairwise respondent similarities based on that aspect's twenty variables. The RV coefficient between aspects $h$ and $k$ is the cosine of the angle between these two similarity structures: $\mathrm{RV}(h,k) = \mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_h \mathbf{S}_k) / \sqrt{\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_h^2)\,\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_k^2)}$. When a block has a single variable, RV reduces to the squared Pearson correlation.} If the three aspects were redundant, all RVs would be high. If they're independent, people who rank highly on one aspect might rank quite differently on another. That independence is what makes complex tastes geometrically possible: a person can like a genre without listening to it, listen without liking, or value highly without either. The empirical question is whether this actually happens.

\subsubsection{Participation of Each Aspect in the Global Space}

Good. The three aspects are independent. But now a second question: when we merge them into one compromise space, do all three actually show up, or does one get swallowed by the others? We use the \textit{$Lg$ coefficient} to find out, measuring how much of each aspect's internal structure survives the merging process. Because we deliberately weighted the aspects to give them equal voice, an unexpectedly high or low $Lg$ would signal trouble---either an aspect didn't mesh well with the others, or it managed to dominate despite the handicap. The $Lg$ is normalized so that perfect equal contribution yields an $Lg$ of approximately $1$ for each aspect. Thus, we're asking: Do all three aspects genuinely leave their fingerprints on the combined space?\footnote{Formally, $Lg(h, \mathrm{MFA})$ is the inner product of the configuration matrix for aspect $h$ with the configuration matrix of the combined MFA, on an absolute scale. The balancing weights ensure that each aspect's first axis contributes approximately equally to the global MFA in terms of inertia, so $Lg$ measures participation in the compromise as a whole.}

\subsubsection{Which Aspect Organizes Each Dimension?}

Suppose we know all three aspects participate in the space. A third question arises: Do they participate equally in every dimension, or does one aspect dominate some dimensions? The \textit{aspect contribution} tells us the answer: on each dimension, what share of the structure comes from each aspect? On Dimension 1, is the geometry mostly about what people like? What they listen to? Or a mix? Contributions sum to $100\%$ per dimension, so we're really asking: Which aspects are pulling in the same direction on this dimension, and where do they diverge? Dimensions where one aspect dominates are exactly where the aspects can separate most clearly, and where complex tastes should leave the clearest fingerprints.\footnote{The contribution of aspect $h$ to dimension $s$ is the sum of the squared coordinates of its twenty variables on that dimension, weighted and normalized by the dimension's overall variance.} 

\subsection{Measuring How Much Individual Tastes Come Apart}

So far we've asked about the space as a whole: How independent are the aspects? Do all three participate? Which aspect participates the most on which dimension? Now we flip back to the individual level, asking: \emph{For each person, on each dimension, how much do their three aspects agree or disagree?}

\subsubsection{Agreement and Disagreement Between Aspects}

To measure within-person disagreement, we proceed as follows. First, note that each person has \textit{three} separate coordinates on each Dimension---one from the separate MCA analyses of their preferences, one from the consumption analysis, plus a third one based on their evaluations---one per aspect. For Dimension 1, let us call these $F_{1,\text{p}}$, $F_{1,\text{c}}$, $F_{1,\text{e}}$. These three aspect-specific coordinates are called that person's three \emph{partial points} on the specified dimension of the compromise space. Their global position on that dimension in the compromise space is the average of these three partial points. Now all three of these points may be very close (and even coincide); alternatively, the three might not be very close. For instance, Person A might have all three coordinates at $+2$ (perfect agreement). Person B might have coordinates at $+3$, $+1$, and $-1$ (strong disagreement).

We measure this disagreement with a score called $W_s(i)$. This score answers the question: ``How much do this person's three aspects disagree on this dimension?'' If all three dimension-specific scores are identical, $W_s(i) = 0$ (simple taste, complete agreement). If they're far apart, $W_s(i)$ is large (complex taste, substantial disagreement).

Mathematically, the following decomposition holds exactly:

\begin{equation}
\sum_{h=1}^{H} F_{sh}(i)^2 \;=\; H \cdot F_s(i)^2 \;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{h=1}^{H} \left(F_{sh}(i) - F_s(i)\right)^2}_{W_s(i)},
\label{eq:decomp}
\end{equation}

Where $F_s(i)$ is the person's global position (where all three aspects place them), $W_s(i)$ is the disagreement score, and $H = 3$ the number of aspects being considered. The first term ($H \cdot F_s(i)^2$) measures the person's position on the dimension---how far they sit from the center; the second term ($W_s(i)$) measures how much that position varies depending on which aspect we look at. To see how much disagreement matters for a dimension as a whole, we sum these individual scores $W_s(i)$ across all respondents $i$. Thus, $\sum_i W_s(i)$ gives us the total within-respondent disagreement on dimension $s$, and dividing by the total inertia on that dimension $\sum_i \sum_h F_{sh}(i)^2$ gives the proportion of the dimension's variance that stems from aspect disagreement versus the respondents' shared positions on the dimension.\footnote{Formally, the dimension-level disagreement share is $\sum_i W_s(i) / \sum_i \sum_h F_{sh}(i)^2$. The denominator follows from Equation~\ref{eq:decomp} summed across all respondents, or $\sum_i \sum_h F_{sh}(i)^2 = \sum_i H \cdot F_s(i)^2 + \sum_i W_s(i)$, so the disagreement share plus the position share sum to one.}

An example makes the decomposition easier to grasp (Figure~\ref{fig:worked-example}). Consider a respondent who likes fifteen of the twenty genres---from jazz, classic rock/oldies, and country to top 40 and heavy metal---listens to nine of them, and credits the fans of eighteen genres with unambiguously high status (a somewhat status-ecumenical person). On the status-valuation axis (the vertical dimension in both panels), the preference and consumption points sit slightly on the withholding side of the origin ($-0.76$ and $-0.96$), while the evaluation point lies far out on the generous side ($+14.42$), since this respondent grants high status to nearly every genre's fans, a generosity of valuation that far outruns both their liking and their listening. The global point is $+4.24$, and the disagreement dwarfs the position: $W_4 = (-0.76 - 4.24)^2 + (-0.96 - 4.24)^2 + (14.42 - 4.24)^2 = 155.7$, or 74\% of the projected partial inertia---nearly everything that places this respondent on the status-valuation dimension is disagreement between aspects, not shared orientation.\footnote{In Ma's combinatorial terms (see Appendix~\ref{app:configurations}), the same respondent holds thirteen genres in complex configurations: one guilty pleasure, seven taste poses, four instances of distant praise, and one instance of distanced consumption.} The volume dimension (the left panel's horizontal axis) tells a second story: all three aspect points cluster tightly between $+2.90$ and $+3.41$, around a global point of $+3.13$, giving $W_2 = 0.1$---essentially zero. All three aspects agree that this is a heavy engager. Finally, on the highbrow--popular dimension (the right panel's horizontal axis), the preference point sits well down the popular side ($-2.61$) while consumption and evaluation sit slightly on the highbrow side ($+0.61$ and $+0.66$), around a global point of $-0.45$. Here the aspects disagree moderately about where on the hierarchy this person sits ($W_1 = 7.0$, 41\% of the projected partial inertia), with liking running ahead of listening toward the popular pole.\footnote{As the discrete complement to this geometric measure, each genre--respondent pair is classified into one of Ma's eight configurations from the binary triple of orientations (preference, consumption, evaluation): the simple taste $(+++)$, the simple non-taste $(---)$, and the six complex tastes (Appendix~\ref{app:configurations}).}

\subsubsection{Pairwise Disagreements and Sources of Complexity}

We can drill down further. The $W_s(i)$ score is made up of three pairwise disagreements: between liking and listening, between liking and evaluations, and between listening and evaluations. Each pairwise distance captures how far apart two aspects place a person on this dimension. The three pairwise distances sum exactly to $H \cdot W_s(i)$, so we can ask: ``Which pair of aspects is responsible for most of the disagreement on this dimension for each individual?'' On Dimension 4 (status valuation), the preference--evaluation and consumption--evaluation distances will likely be large (evaluations place people far from where liking/listening do). On Dimension 2 (volume), they might be more balanced.\footnote{The squared pairwise distance between aspects $h$ and $k$ is simply $(F_{sh}(i) - F_{sk}(i))^2$. The three distances sum exactly to $H \cdot W_s(i)$.}

Pairwise disagreements capture which aspects pull against each other, but they don't distinguish two very different mechanisms by which a person's taste becomes complex. A respondent might hold contradictory opinions of a single genre---liking it but not valuing it highly, for instance---or the same kind of disagreement might appear across multiple genres in a way that cancels out. We can decompose $W_s(i)$ to separate these two sources of disagreement.

\begin{equation}
W_s(i) \;=\; \underbrace{\sum_{g=1}^{G} H^2 \sum_{h=1}^{H} d_{ighs}^2}_{\substack{\omega_s(i;g) \\ \text{genre-based}}} \;+\; \underbrace{2H^2 \sum_{g < g'} \sum_{h=1}^{H} d_{ighs} d_{ig'hs}}_{\substack{\gamma_s(i) \\ \text{coherence}}}
\label{eq:genre}
\end{equation}

The first term, $\sum_g \omega_s(i;g)$, captures the respondent's \emph{genre-based complex taste}. The deviations $d_{ighs} = c_{ighs} - c_{gs}$ measure how far each respondent's partial point for aspect $h$ deviates from that genre's category coordinate on dimension $s$. Here, $c_{ighs}$ is the respondent's score from the separate MCA for aspect $h$ on dimension $s$, projected into the global MFA coordinate system---the mechanism that makes partial points aspect-specific, since the global MFA produces only dimension-specific scores per respondent, while the three partial points come from separate analyses of preference, consumption, and evaluation. The term $c_{gs}$ is the category coordinate for genre $g$ on dimension $s$, which by MFA duality equals the mean of individual partial points for that genre. For example, if the preference partial sits at $+2$, consumption at $-1$, and evaluation at $+3$ while a genre's category coordinate sits at $0$, the three deviations are $+2$, $-1$, and $+3$, and their squared sum $\omega_s(i;g)$ is large. Summed across all twenty genres, $\sum_g \omega_s(i;g)$ captures total genre-based disagreement. This component is large when a respondent's three aspects contradict each other within specific genres---when, for example, a person likes a genre but doesn't value it (a guilty pleasure), or values it without listening (distant praise).

The second term, $\gamma_s(i)$, captures \emph{cross-genre coherence}: whether the per-genre deviations $d_{ighs}$ point in the same direction across genres (reinforcing disagreement) or in opposite directions (cancelling disagreement). Formally, it sums the products of deviations for each genre pair and aspect: if a respondent deviates positively for genre $g$ and negatively for genre $g'$ on the same aspect, the product is negative and reduces total disagreement. If the deviations both point the same way, the product is positive and increases it. Positive $\gamma_s(i)$ means per-genre disagreements reinforce each other; negative $\gamma_s(i)$ means they cancel. 

To illustrate: imagine a respondent who (on a particular dimension) prefers genre $g$ above its genre coordinate but consumption places them below it. On a different genre $g'$, the opposite happens: consumption pulls them above, preference below. When summed across all genres, these disagreements partially cancel, yielding negative $\gamma_s(i)$ that reduces the total $W_s(i)$. Conversely, if the same respondent shows the same type of disagreement (say, consumption always above the genre coordinate, preference always below) repeated across many genres, disagreements reinforce each other, yielding large positive $\gamma_s(i)$ that amplifies $W_s(i)$. A person with high $\gamma_s(i)$ shows a \emph{consistent} pattern of contradiction across many genres; one with high $\omega_s(i;g)$ shows intense contradiction within specific genres but potentially low $\gamma_s(i)$.

Examples illuminate both components and reveal the diversity of disagreement profiles. Table~\ref{tab:respondent-typology} presents three ideal-type respondents arrayed from low to high disagreement on the status-valuation dimension, showing how the same geometric mechanisms produce different outcomes. Respondent 522 (a low-disagreement case) likes five genres, listens to four, and grants high status to eleven, with all three aspect points clustering tightly around $F_4 = -0.36$; their $W_4 = 1.1$ consists almost entirely of genre-based disagreement (0.8) with minimal coherence ($\gamma_4 = +0.3$). Respondent 362 (the high case, discussed in detail below) displays the high-coherence profile: $W_4 = 155.7$ splits into only 11.2 genre-based and 144.4 coherence ($\gamma_4 = 144.4$), meaning 93\% of disagreement stems from per-genre contradictions that reinforce each other across all twenty genres. By contrast, a hypothetical third respondent might hold high genre-based disagreement (say, $\omega_4 = 50$ across multiple genres where they like but don't value, or vice versa) with negative $\gamma_4$ that mostly cancels it out, yielding a moderate or low total score despite holding many individual contradictions. These three mechanisms---tight clustering, reinforcing contradictions, and cancelling contradictions---show that respondents with identical configuration counts can have vastly different $W_s(i)$ scores, and vice versa.

These geometric measures are complementary to a simpler approach: counting how many genres a respondent holds in each of Ma's eight configurations (guilty pleasures, taste poses, distant praise, and so on). That combinatorial measure answers a different question---\emph{how many} genres exhibit each type of complex configuration---whereas $W_s(i)$ answers how much disagreement matters \emph{on each dimension}. As the results show (discussed below in Section~\ref{sec:antinomies}), the two measures correlate weakly and reveal different patterns. Respondent 362 holds thirteen complex configurations, yet their disagreement scores on the volume and musical-family dimensions are essentially zero ($W_2 = 0.1$, $W_3 = 0.3$)---on those dimensions their liking, listening, and evaluating place them together---while nearly all of their disagreement concentrates on the status-valuation dimension ($W_4 = 155.7$). Conversely, the geometric approach captures both the magnitude of disagreement and its structure: whether it arises from isolated genre-specific contradictions or from a coherent, repeated pattern across genres. This decomposition enables analysis of how social position shapes not just \emph{whether} people disagree, but \emph{how} and \emph{where} they disagree.

\section{Results}

\subsection{Overall Structure of the Complex Taste Space}

How large and clear are the patterns in the complex taste space? Table~\ref{tab:eigen} shows that the first dimension captures $8.23\%$ of the variation, the second $7.25\%$, the third $5.39\%$, the fourth $5.11\%$, and the first five dimensions together $30.35\%$. These percentages are typical for data like ours---binary yes/no responses scattered across twenty genres analyzed via MCA. Much of the variation is genre-specific (whether you like opera has little to do with whether you like hip-hop), so no single dimension captures huge amounts. In the Geometric Data Analysis tradition, this variation is called \emph{inertia}---the total spread or dispersion of the respondent cloud around its center. When we say a dimension captures $8.23\%$ of the inertia, we mean that ordering respondents along that dimension explains $8.23\%$ of how different they are from one another. All analyses were conducted in \textsf{R} using the \textsf{FactoMineR} package, and scripts reproducing all results are available in the replication materials.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering \caption{Eigenvalues of the MFA (first five dimensions).}
\label{tab:eigen}

\end{table}

The category coordinates reveal what each dimension means; they are shown in Figure~\ref{fig:categories1-2}. On the first dimension, the preference and consumption yes categories split cleanly along the traditional prestige hierarchy. The consecrated genres sit on the positive side (for consumption, opera at $+0.72$, big band at $+0.69$, classical music at $+0.64$; for preference, opera at $+0.61$), while the popular genres sit on the negative side (rap/hip-hop at $-1.26$, indie rock at $-1.29$ for consumption). Whether we measure liking or listening, the same genres cluster together---the classic \emph{highbrow--popular hierarchy} that researchers have documented for decades \citep{bourdieu1984distinction,jæger2024from-a4b}. The hierarchy is strongly anchored in generation \citep{lizardo2015musical-8c6}, with older people tending toward the highbrow pole and younger people toward the popular pole (Section~\ref{sec:social}). Status attributions, by contrast, barely move along this dimension (evaluation yes categories range from $-0.23$ for rap/hip-hop to $+0.39$ for dance/club music). Dimension 1 is thus a \emph{highbrow--popular} axis.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig-categories-d12} \caption{Category map of the MFA (dimensions 1--2). Colored points are the ``yes'' categories of each aspect; grey points are the corresponding ``no'' categories. On Dimension 1 the preference and consumption ``yes'' categories split highbrow (right) from popular (left); on Dimension 2 (volume) all of them sit on the positive side, the rarest engagements furthest from the origin. Evaluation ``yes'' categories barely spread on either axis.}
\label{fig:categories1-2}
\end{figure}

Dimension 2 is a \emph{volume} axis, ordered by how much respondents engage at all. Every preference and consumption yes category sits on the positive side, and the rarer the engagement, the further out the category sits. Listening to folk ($+1.35$), bluegrass ($+1.31$), or big band ($+1.19$) places a respondent far along the axis, while listening to rap/hip-hop ($+0.05$) or heavy metal ($+0.03$) barely moves it, because those engagements are widespread. Liking follows the same rarity ordering (folk at $+0.84$, big band at $+0.80$, opera at $+0.78$ at the extremes). Evaluation yes categories follow rarity as well---granting status to blues/R\&B fans ($+0.59$), Latin/salsa fans ($+0.57$), or heavy metal fans ($+0.51$) is more distinctive than granting it to classical music fans ($+0.03$)---but they stay far closer to the origin than the engagement categories. Where respondents sit on this axis thus depends on the sheer volume of their engagement.

Dimension 3 separates genres by musical family rather than by prestige. The consumption yes categories for the Black, Latin, and Caribbean diaspora genres sit at the positive pole---reggae at $+0.95$, Latin/salsa at $+0.76$, rap/hip-hop at $+0.61$---while the guitar-rock cluster sits at the negative pole (heavy metal at $-0.91$, indie rock at $-0.76$). Liking mirrors the same contrast (rap/hip-hop at $+0.60$, Latin/salsa at $+0.51$, reggae at $+0.45$, against heavy metal at $-0.62$ and indie rock at $-0.53$), while evaluation is nearly silent (its yes categories span only $-0.33$ to $+0.17$). Where respondents sit on this dimension depends on which family of music they engage, and the dimension is strongly anchored in race and ethnicity (Section~\ref{sec:social}).

The vertical axis of the category map in Figure~\ref{fig:categories} (Dimension 4) tells a different story. All twenty evaluation yes categories sit clustered on the positive side of the origin. The preference and consumption yes categories, by contrast, scatter around zero. On this dimension, the rarer the high-status attribution for a genre, the higher that genre sits (rap/hip-hop and Latin/salsa at $+1.94$, against $+0.02$ for classical music and $+0.00$ for opera)---popular genres receive high-status attributions from fewer respondents, making their fans appear as distinctive high-status recipients. This is the \emph{status-valuation} dimension, almost entirely an evaluation axis. A respondent's position here depends almost solely on how they distribute status recognition across genres' fans, independent of their liking or listening. Generous respondents---those who grant high status to fans of most genres---sit high on the vertical axis, while respondents who reserve high status for traditionally consecrated genres (like classical or opera) sit low.

Dimension 3 separates musical families, with the diaspora genres' consumption and liking categories on the positive side and the guitar-rock cluster on the negative side. Dimension 4 is the status-valuation axis: all evaluation ``yes'' categories sit on the positive pole, ordered by rarity, while preference and consumption ``yes'' categories cluster near the origin.}

\subsection{Independence or Redundancy Among Complex Taste Aspects}

The Analytic Strategy section asked: Are the three aspects distinct or the same thing measured three ways? The RV coefficients answer the question empirically. Preference and consumption rank respondents quite similarly (RV = 0.35), but not identically. If you like a lot of genres, you probably listen to a lot too. But not everyone who listens a lot likes a lot, and vice versa---the two are far from perfectly correlated.

Evaluation, though, is a different story. It shows an RV of $0.014$ with preference and $0.015$ with consumption. These near-zero values are the key empirical finding: evaluations rank respondents almost completely independently of their liking and listening. Knowing whether someone likes many genres tells you virtually nothing about whether they grant high status to genres' fans. The three aspects are genuinely distinct. What you like, what you listen to, and what you praise are three separable dimensions of taste. This is why complex tastes exist: a person can like a genre without listening to it, listen without liking, or evaluate highly without either liking or listening. None of these patterns is surprising or contradictory. They're the natural result of the three aspects being partially independent.

\subsection{How Each Aspect Participates in Each Dimension}

We've seen that all three aspects contribute to the global space, but they don't contribute equally to every dimension. Let's walk through what each dimension reveals.

\emph{Dimension 1---the highbrow--popular axis.} This dimension captures the genre hierarchy, with opera, classical, and big band sitting on the positive side and rap, indie rock, and metal on the negative side. It's driven almost entirely by what people listen to and what they like (correlations of $-0.83$ and $-0.89$ with the aspect axes), while evaluations barely move ($1.1\%$ of the variation). This makes sense: liking and listening are the places where the genre hierarchy shows up most sharply.

\emph{Dimension 2---the volume axis.} This dimension captures how intensely people engage with music overall. Preference and consumption dominate here (correlations of $+0.83$ and $+0.73$), while evaluation's separate structure appears only weakly ($+0.23$ correlation, $4.2\%$ of the variation). Heavy engagers sit on the positive side, light engagers on the negative.

\emph{Dimension 3---the musical-family contrast.} This is where reggae, Latin/salsa, and rap sit on the positive side, while metal, indie rock, and traditional country-rock occupy the negative side. Again, consumption and preference drive almost everything ($+0.94$ and $+0.88$ correlations), while evaluation barely registers ($3.1\%$ contribution). This dimension captures something like diasporic music versus English-language rock---a cultural family distinction that shows up in how people actually engage.

\emph{Dimension 4---the status-valuation axis.} Here the pattern shifts dramatically. This dimension correlates almost perfectly with evaluation ($+0.95$) while liking and listening barely move ($< 0.05$ correlation for both). Where people sit on this dimension is determined almost entirely by how they evaluate genres' fans. Respondents' tastes in the first three dimensions would tell you virtually nothing about their status attributions---that's a separate story entirely.

This fourth dimension is the most striking finding. It shows that evaluation is not just another perspective on the same taste space; it's genuinely independent. Your taste position on genres (where you sit on the hierarchy and how intensely you engage) tells us almost nothing about whether you grant high status to their fans.

\subsection{Which Aspect Dominates Each Dimension?}
\label{sec:contrib}

We've seen these four dimensions in broad strokes. Now let's look at the numbers: how much of each dimension's variation comes from each aspect? Table~\ref{tab:groups} shows the aspect contributions---the percentage share of each dimension---alongside the $Lg$ coefficients that measure overall participation.

The numbers confirm the visual picture. Dimension 1 (highbrow--popular) is consumption-dominated at 54.6\%, with preference contributing 44.3\% and evaluation a bare 1.1\%. Dimension 2 (volume) is preference-dominant at 52.3\%, with consumption at 43.4\% and evaluation modestly at 4.2\%. Dimension 3 (musical family) again leans consumption-heavy at 56.3\%, with preference at 40.5\% and evaluation minimal at 3.1\%. But Dimension 4 breaks the pattern entirely: evaluation overwhelms at 91.1\%, with preference and consumption each contributing only around 4\%.

What's really happening here is this. Liking and listening put respondents on two fundamentally shared ladders---where they rank on the genre hierarchy (highbrow versus popular music) and how intensely they engage overall (volume). A third dimension splits genres by cultural family, the diaspora and Latin music cluster against the English-language rock family. Then evaluation steps in and does something completely different. The evaluation categories are ordered by how rare it is to grant a particular genre's fans high status. Rap fans? Distinctive to elevate. Opera fans? Nearly everyone does it, so no variation there. This creates a dimension measuring respondents' generosity or withholding of recognition---their willingness to extend prestige downward in the hierarchy. That's what Dimension 4 captures. Respondents' positions on the first three dimensions---their genre preferences, their listening intensity, their cultural geography---tell you almost nothing about where they land on the fourth. Evaluation is its own story.

\subsection{Measuring Complex Tastes}
\label{sec:antinomies}

Now we get to the core question: \emph{For each person, on each dimension, how much do their three aspects disagree?} We measure this with the score $W_s(i)$ (Equation~\ref{eq:decomp}), the dispersion of a person's three partial coordinates around their global position---the average location of those three aspect-specific coordinates. It's zero when all three aspects place them at the same location (simple taste) and grows as they place them further apart (complex taste).

What's surprising is how much complex tastes matter geometrically. On Dimension 1, the disagreement score accounts for 49\% of the total variation (inertia) on that dimension---meaning that 49\% of the variation comes from respondents' aspects disagreeing with each other, and 51\% comes from where respondents sit in the space when we average their three aspect positions (their global position).\footnote{These percentages are computed by summing the individual aspect-disagreement scores across all respondents, $\sum_i W_s(i)$, and dividing by the total inertia on that dimension: $\frac{\sum_i W_s(i)}{\sum_i \sum_h F_{sh}(i)^2}$, where $F_{sh}(i)$ is aspect $h$'s coordinate for respondent $i$ on dimension $s$. From Equation~\ref{eq:decomp}, the two components (aspect disagreement and global position) partition the total inertia exactly.} On Dimension 2, it's 55\% disagreement versus 45\% global position. On Dimension 3, it's 52\% disagreement versus 48\% global position. On Dimension 4, it's 66\% disagreement versus 34\% global position. This means aspect disagreement is roughly as important as where respondents sit when their aspects agree (their global position) in shaping the structure of the space. Complex tastes aren't a marginal phenomenon confined to a few unusual respondents. They're woven throughout the structure of the space.

But there's another way to measure complex tastes, one that counts instead of measuring. Ma's framework identifies eight configurations that people hold in individual genres: guilty pleasures, taste poses, distanced consumption, and so on (Appendix~\ref{app:configurations} defines them). You can tally how many of a person's 20 genres fall into complex configurations---a combinatorial count. How does this count relate to the geometric $W_s(i)$ score?

The correlations are interesting. Configuration count versus $W_s(i)$: on Dimension 1, $\rho = 0.17$; on Dimension 2, $\rho = 0.28$; on Dimension 3, $\rho = 0.18$; on Dimension 4, $\rho = -0.11$. Surprisingly weak, and the strongest correlation is with the volume dimension. Why? The configuration count is dimension-free---it just tallies how many genres you hold in contradictory configurations. The geometric score, by contrast, is dimension-specific: it measures how much disagreement matters on the axis you're looking at. They're answering different questions. Figure~\ref{fig:signatures} shows the geometric signatures of each configuration type. Each configuration occupies a distinct region of the space. But there's substantial variation within each configuration. Respondents with guilty pleasures, for instance, range widely on the status-valuation disagreement score---mean $W_4$ of $4.5$, but SD of $10.4$. Some people hold their guilty pleasure in intense contradiction across their three aspects; others barely do. The same configuration can manifest very differently depending on which genres hold it and how strongly the aspects disagree within those genres.\footnote{The supplementary Figure~\ref{fig:config-variation} in the appendix visualizes the full range of within-configuration variation across all eight configurations and four dimensions.}

Heatmap shows Spearman correlations between configuration counts (per respondent, out of 20 genres) and MFA coordinates and complex-taste scores ($N = 2{,}259$), across four dimensions and three score types (global coordinates, aspect-disagreement, genre-based complex taste).}

\subsection{The Social Sources of Complex Tastes}
\label{sec:social}

A fundamental question: \emph{Who has complex tastes?} We know taste positions are socially stratified---older people like highbrow music, younger people popular, and so forth \citep{bourdieu1984distinction,bennett2009culture-aef}. But are people who experience disagreement between their aspects concentrated in particular demographic groups, or scattered throughout?

Here's the surprising finding: complex tastes are scattered everywhere. When we model the disagreement scores $W_s(i)$ using demographics, we find that age, education, income, race, class, gender, parents' education, and region together explain only $4.4\%$ of the variation in $W_1$ (highbrow--popular), $3.6\%$ in $W_2$ (volume), $10.0\%$ in $W_3$ (musical-family), and $1.9\%$ in $W_4$ (status valuation). 

Compare that to taste position, which is demographics-driven. Your global position on the genre hierarchy ($\eta^2$ ranging from 0.01 to 0.31) is predictable from your age and education. Researchers can forecast fairly accurately whether you lean highbrow or popular \citep{lizardo2015musical-8c6}. But aspect disagreement? Far more opaque. No demographic profile reliably predicts whether your liking, listening, and evaluations will line up or diverge. It's as if complex taste is woven throughout the population rather than concentrated in any particular social location.

The few effects that do appear show distinct patterns by dimension. On the highbrow--popular axis ($W_1$), younger respondents show less disagreement (ages 30--39: $b = -0.82$, $p < .001$; ages 60--69: $b = -1.59$, $p < .001$), while region effects appear (South: $b = -0.42$, $p = .030$; West: $b = -0.60$, $p < .001$). On the volume dimension ($W_2$), upper-class respondents show substantially elevated disagreement ($b = 4.54$, $p < .001$), as do those with college-educated parents ($b = 1.52$, $p < .001$). On the musical-family contrast ($W_3$), race/ethnicity dominates: Black respondents show higher disagreement ($b = 1.61$, $p < .001$), as do those identifying with multiple races ($b = 1.41$, $p < .001$) and Hispanic respondents ($b = 0.52$, $p < .001$); older respondents show less disagreement (ages 60--69 and 70+: $b = -0.77$ and $-0.93$, both $p < .001$). On the status-valuation dimension ($W_4$), upper-class respondents dominate ($b = 9.16$, $p < .001$), and middle-aged respondents show elevated scores (ages 30--39 and 40--49: $b = 2.42$ and $2.31$, both $p < .05$). The overall pattern is clear: different dimensions of disagreement are anchored by different demographics. The three aspects---liking, listening, evaluating---are weakly coupled overall, yet their specific patterns of disagreement vary by the dimension and the demographic group.

But this seemingly weak overall social patterning masks an important distinction. Recall that the disagreement score $W_s(i)$ decomposes into two components (Equation~\ref{eq:genre}): the \emph{genre-based} part $\sum_g \omega_s(i;g)$, which sums up how much a respondent's three aspects disagree within each of the twenty genres, and the \emph{cross-genre coherence} component $\gamma_s(i)$, which measures whether those per-genre disagreements reinforce or cancel each other across the full repertoire. To illustrate: a respondent might have high genre-based disagreement in rap (likes it, doesn't listen regularly, withholds status) and simultaneously in operatic music (doesn't like it, listens out of cultural obligation, grants status)---these work against each other in the total score when $\gamma_s(i)$ is negative, or together when it's positive. 

These two components of disagreement show strikingly different social patterns. The genre-based component is substantially more socially structured, with demographics explaining $22.2\%$, $7.9\%$, $20.1\%$, and $3.0\%$ of its variation across the four dimensions (compared to $4.4\%$, $3.6\%$, $10.0\%$, and $1.9\%$ for the total scores). Upper-class respondents show elevated genre-based disagreement on the volume dimension, and race/ethnicity strongly anchors the genre-based component on the musical-family contrast. The cross-genre coherence component $\gamma_s(i)$---whether per-genre disagreements align or cancel---is more weakly structured overall, with $R^2$ values around $3.5\%$, $3.5\%$, $7.1\%$, and $1.8\%$ across the four dimensions. Social position thus shapes which genres anchor the genre-based component of disagreement, while coherence follows a weaker patterning of its own. Section~\ref{sec:coherence} examines the coherence component directly.

\subsection{Which Genres Anchor Complex Tastes? Demographic Concentration}
\label{sec:genre-specificity}

Figures~\ref{fig:omega-demographics-d1}--\ref{fig:omega-demographics-d4} map genre-specific disagreement visually, one figure per dimension of the complex taste space. The eight genres shown are those in which the demographic patterns concentrate most sharply---rap/hip-hop, indie rock, and dance/club for the age gradient on the highbrow--popular dimension, big band at its older pole, classical music, opera, and musicals for the education and class effects, and Latin/salsa for the largest race-indicator effect in the survey. Every cell reports the Pearson correlation between a demographic variable and the genre's genre-based component $\omega$: own education and subjective class as four category indicators each, age, parental education, and gender as measured, and race and ethnicity as category indicators. Census region shows no genre-specific concentration anywhere in the taste space (no correlation reaches $|r| = 0.10$), so it is omitted. Blue cells indicate positive correlations (more genre-specific disagreement among respondents in that category); red cells indicate negative correlations. 

Which socio-demographic groups experience disagreement relative to which genres? We organize findings by the four dimensions.

\emph{On the highbrow--popular dimension}, age creates the sharpest patterns. Younger respondents hold more genre-based disagreement in the popular genres---rap/hip-hop ($r = -0.44$), indie rock ($-0.36$), heavy metal ($-0.27$), and dance/club ($-0.25$)---while older respondents show more in folk ($0.22$) and big band ($0.18$). Race and ethnicity matter here as well. Hispanic respondents show elevated disagreement in Latin/salsa ($r = 0.44$), and White respondents show the mirror image in Latin/salsa ($-0.34$), rap/hip-hop ($-0.27$), and reggae ($-0.22$). Black respondents show elevated disagreement in gospel ($0.25$), blues ($0.23$), and rap/hip-hop ($0.20$). Postgraduate respondents show somewhat more disagreement in opera ($r = 0.17$).

\emph{On the volume dimension}, the same race and age contrasts appear in somewhat weaker form (Hispanic respondents in Latin/salsa, $r = 0.34$, against $-0.30$ for White respondents; older respondents in big band, $0.19$, and younger in indie rock, $-0.21$), alongside an education gradient in the consecrated genres. Postgraduate respondents show elevated genre-based disagreement in opera ($r = 0.17$) and musicals ($0.15$), and respondents with college-educated parents show it in opera, classical music, and musicals ($r = 0.12$ each). Upper-class respondents show elevated disagreement in opera ($r = 0.15$), though their other correlations are small.

\emph{On the musical-family dimension}, the age and race patterns of the first dimension recur at nearly the same strength (rap/hip-hop $r = -0.44$ and indie rock $-0.34$ for age; Latin/salsa $0.43$ for Hispanic respondents against $-0.34$ for White; blues $0.26$ and rap/hip-hop $0.20$ for Black respondents). The overlap reflects the two dimensions' shared basis in liking and listening. The musical-family dimension nevertheless adds its own reading, since the disagreement it registers concentrates in the contrast between the diaspora genres and the guitar-rock cluster, the axis most strongly anchored in race and ethnicity (Section~\ref{sec:social}).

\emph{On the status-valuation dimension}, the associations are weak throughout, consistent with demographics explaining little of the variation in that component ($R^2 = 3.0\%$). The largest correlations are postgraduate respondents in opera ($r = 0.18$) and older respondents in big band ($0.16$); no other correlation reaches $|r| = 0.15$.

The genre-based component thus becomes a window onto how demographic position works. It shapes not just whether people sit on the highbrow or popular side of the genre hierarchy (taste position), but \emph{where} and \emph{how} their aspects come apart (taste structure). Social location doesn't uniformly make people's aspects disagree more or less; instead, it directs that disagreement toward specific cultural objects. Demographics channel complex tastes through particular genres that carry social meaning and group identity.

The eight-genre matrices above foreground the largest demographic effects; the supplementary appendix (Figures~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d1}--\ref{fig:omega-genres-d4}) extends these to all twenty genres and all sixteen demographic indicators, showing where the patterns hold and where they fade. The full matrices reveal that the demographic shaping of disagreement is genuinely genre-specific: each demographic group's complex tastes concentrate in a distinct subset of the repertoire, and few correlations exceed $|r| = 0.15$ outside the genres highlighted above. This pattern validates the interpretive claim: demographics shape which genres people find disagreeable, not whether they experience disagreement.

\subsection{The Social Patterning of Cross-Genre Coherence}
\label{sec:coherence}

The genre-based component is socially patterned: age, race, education, and class channel disagreement into different genres. But what about the coherence component---the reinforcing or cancelling of per-genre disagreements across the full repertoire? 

We tested this with the same demographic variables and methods. The pattern is striking in its near-absence: bivariate associations are tiny. Gender shows nothing anywhere. Only one association reaches even $\eta^2 = 0.05$---race/ethnicity on the musical-family dimension at $0.049$, which is also the dimension where race most strongly shapes the genres themselves. The total disagreement scores show the same near-null pattern: their largest bivariate association is also race on the musical-family dimension ($\eta^2 = 0.064$). Coherence, like aspect disagreement itself, is not the signature of any particular demographic group.

The joint regression models tell the same story with a little more structure. Demographics explain $3.5\%$ of the variation in $\gamma_1$ (highbrow--popular), $3.5\%$ in $\gamma_2$ (volume), $7.1\%$ in $\gamma_3$ (musical-family), and $1.8\%$ in $\gamma_4$ (status)---weaker than the genre-based component's $22.2\%$, $7.9\%$, $20.1\%$, and $3.0\%$. The effects that do appear concentrate on $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_3$. On the highbrow--popular dimension, coherence declines across the middle age cohorts ($b = -1.12$ at ages 50--59, $p < .001$), though the oldest cohort no longer differs from the youngest, and postgraduate respondents show somewhat more coherence ($b = 0.61$, $p < .05$). On the musical-family dimension, race dominates: Black respondents show substantially higher coherence ($b = 1.43$, $p < .001$), as do respondents identifying with more than one race ($b = 0.99$, $p < .01$), while the Midwest and West show slightly lower coherence ($b = -0.40$ and $-0.55$, both $p < .05$). The volume dimension's few effects---coherence higher among respondents with college-educated parents ($b = 1.33$, $p < .001$) and among upper-class respondents---belong to the class story taken up below. The status-valuation dimension shows the least structure of all ($R^2 = 1.8\%$). Gender and household income show nothing reliable on any dimension.

Because Equation~\ref{eq:genre} is an identity, and the coherence models use the same sample and predictors as the models for the total scores, every coefficient in Section~\ref{sec:social} splits exactly into a genre-based and a coherent part. This attribution sharpens the reading of the class and family-background results. The upper-class premium on $W_2$ (volume: $b = 4.54$) is almost entirely coherence ($b = 4.09$), with only a small genre-based part ($b = 0.45$). Upper-class respondents' disagreement on the volume dimension, in other words, does not take the form of contradictions lodged in particular genres. It takes the form of a repertoire-wide alignment, with the same aspect displaced in the same direction across genre after genre, so that the per-genre deviations reinforce one another instead of cancelling. This is the empirical counterpart of the toy contrast in the analytic strategy---the same total disagreement can be assembled from a single genre held in intense contradiction or from twenty genres tilted the same way, and social position helps decide which assembly a person's disagreement takes.

Coherence is not always reinforcing. Substantial proportions of respondents show negative coherence, meaning their per-genre disagreements partially cancel and their total disagreement is smaller than the sum of its genre-level parts: about a third on the highbrow--popular dimension ($33\%$), a quarter on the volume dimension ($25\%$), and more than half on the musical-family dimension ($52\%$). One caveat concerns the status-valuation dimension. Evaluation is the only aspect that varies there, so a respondent who grants high status to many genres displaces their evaluation point in the same direction for every genre at once. For such respondents, much of what $\gamma_4$ records is this uniform displacement rather than configural contradiction, which is why $\gamma_4$ correlates with the magnitude of the global position ($r = 0.78$) more strongly than any other coherence score. Where coherence has social structure, then, it reflects these repertoire-wide orientations rather than localized contradiction. The genre-anchored form of complex taste---the kind whose social geography the previous section mapped---is the genre-based component's contribution.

\subsection{The Duality: Genres as Targets of Complex Tastes}
\label{sec:duality}

Complex tastes have a dual structure. We've traced them from the individual perspective: \emph{who} has complex tastes, and \emph{what} aspects disagree. But genres are targets too. Which genres attract complex tastes? The answer: some genres generate much simpler responses than others.\footnote{At the genre level, we measure the proportion of respondents with simple tastes: those whose three aspects all agree (either all yes---like, listen, grant status---or all no). The complement is the proportion with complex tastes in that genre (any mismatch across aspects).}

Heavy metal, Latin/salsa, and bluegrass produce largely simple tastes: $70\%$, $67\%$, and $65\%$ of respondents respond consistently across all three aspects. You either like them and listen and value them, or you don't. Classical and opera are different. Only $33\%$ and $24\%$ of respondents respond simply to these genres. The rest hold them in contradiction: they might like classical music but rarely listen to it, or they listen out of cultural obligation while withholding judgments about the fans, or they think the music lacks status yet listen regularly. These prestige genres splinter audiences into complex configurations.

To answer this, we need a different analysis. The first MFA treated respondents as the units being analyzed and genres as variables. Now we flip that: rows become genres and columns become respondent-responses (each respondent's yes/no on liking, listening, and evaluation for each genre). We re-run the MFA with genres as units. This is not simply a rearrangement of the original solution; it is a fundamentally different analysis that asks new questions. In the original analysis, genres appeared only as variables; we could locate them through the composition of their audiences---the average profile of people who affirm them. But we cannot compute aspect-level agreement from the respondent analysis alone. Specifically, we cannot ask whether genres that are \emph{liked by many} are also \emph{listened to by many}---that is, whether the liking and listening audiences for each genre overlap. We also cannot see whether different aspects place individual genres in different positions. Both questions require treating genres as the units of analysis and respondents as the indicators.

Technically, this flip changes the analysis fundamentally. Because MFA weights each block inversely to its separate analysis's strength in the first dimension, and transposing reshuffles which variables define the blocks, the balancing weights change: the transposed separate analyses yield different first eigenvalues ($\lambda_1' = 0.153/0.161/0.419$ for preference/consumption/evaluation respondent-indicators, versus the original $0.155/0.127/0.194$ for genre-indicators). The transposed dimensions are thus optimized for spreading genres apart, not respondents. The key statistics we want---RV coefficients comparing aspects at the genre level, and aspect-specific partial points showing where different respondent-groups place each genre---do not exist in the respondent-level fit.\footnote{The transposed MFA was implemented by direct application of the algorithm in \citet{pages2014mfa} and validated by reproducing the respondent-level analysis: eigenvalues, global and partial coordinates, RV coefficients, and group contributions are numerically consistent.}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig-genre-map-d12} \caption{Genre map from the transposed MFA (dimensions 1--2). Black points: genre compromise positions; colored points: aspect partial points (segments connect each genre's compromise to its aspect-specific positions).}
\label{fig:genre-map-d12}
\end{figure}

Here's what's striking: From the genre perspective, the aspects \emph{agree} far more strongly. The RV coefficients jump to $0.92$ (preference and consumption nearly identical), $0.53$ (preference and evaluation), and $0.48$ (consumption and evaluation)---much higher than the individual-level $0.35$, $0.01$, and $0.02$. At the genre level, people who like a genre tend to listen to it and grant its fans high status. Genres that recruit likers recruit listeners too.

But this doesn't contradict what we found at the individual level---it's the ecological fallacy in reverse. The liking audience and the listening audience overlap substantially for each genre. But the \emph{same individuals} don't always inhabit both groups. The person who likes opera but doesn't listen is in the liking audience; the person who listens but doesn't like is in the listening audience. Separately, they agree. Together, at the aggregate genre level, they agree. But at the individual level, people split apart. Complex tastes aren't something genres do; they're something individuals experience. Which individuals respond simply and which complexly varies person by person.

\centering \caption{Genre target profiles: percentage of respondents holding each genre in each of Ma's configurations ($N = 2{,}259$).}
\label{tab:genre-profile}
\input{tables/tab-genre-profile}
\end{table}

The transposed space is itself strongly structured ($\lambda_1 = 2.25$, $14.8\%$ of the inertia; $\lambda_2 = 1.93$, $12.8\%$; $\lambda_3 = 1.25$, $8.2\%$; $\lambda_4 = 1.12$, $7.4\%$), with the first four dimensions accounting for $43.2\%$ of the total variation. The first two dimensions are shown in Figure~\ref{fig:genre-map-d12}, and the fourth dimension is shown in Figure~\ref{fig:genre-map-d14}. 

The first dimension opposes genres whose typical relation is status without engagement---classical ($-3.6$), opera ($-3.0$), and musicals ($-2.1$), with distant-praise rates correlating at $\rho = -0.82$ and taste-pose rates at $\rho = -0.58$---against genres most often held in the guilty pleasure ($\rho = +0.75$)\footnote{The correlation coefficients ($\rho$) reported throughout this section are Spearman rank correlations between each genre's coordinate on the transposed dimension and the genre-level prevalence (proportion of respondents, across all 2,259) who hold that genre in each of Ma's eight configuration types. For example, $\rho = +0.75$ for guilty pleasure on Dimension 1 means that genres with high positive coordinates on that dimension tend to have high prevalence of guilty pleasure configurations, while genres with negative coordinates tend to have low prevalence of that configuration.} and distanced consumption ($+0.80$) configurations. These last include top 40 ($+2.0$), rap/hip-hop ($+1.8$), classic rock/oldies ($+1.3$), and contemporary rock ($+1.3$)---familiar genres most often held with engaged disagreement. This dimension, in plain terms, measures the \emph{engagement--detachment} contrast at the genre level: on the negative side sit prestige genres whose audiences are defined partly by abstention from engagement (the listener who values classical music highly but rarely listens), while the positive side includes genres where respondents' disagreement arises from active engagement despite reservations about status (the guilty-pleasure listener who loves the genre but withholds attributing high status to the genre's audience). In effect, this dimension answers the question: Does a genre recruit audiences through engagement or through distant admiration?

The second dimension is a \emph{configuration axis}: genres are ordered by the complex-taste profiles they attract (Table~\ref{tab:genre-profile}; Figure~\ref{fig:genre-map-d12}). At the positive pole sit the genres respondents actively hold---in simple positive taste ($\rho = +0.77$), as taste poses ($+0.55$), as guilty pleasures ($+0.44$), or as justified abstentions ($+0.44$)---led by classic rock/oldies ($+3.7$), mood/easy listening ($+2.0$), country ($+1.8$), and top 40/pop ($+1.3$). At the negative pole sit genres whose dominant relation is simple non-taste ($\rho = -0.73$): rap/hip-hop ($-1.7$), reggae ($-1.5$), latin/Spanish/salsa ($-1.3$), and heavy metal ($-1.3$)---together with opera ($-1.2$), whose characteristic relation to its audience is instead dominated by distant praise (with $58.9\%$ of respondents holding it in that configuration). The duality is asymmetric in exactly the way complex-taste theory anticipates: the prototypical guilty-pleasure genres are among the least credited with high status (evaluation rates of $8$--$14\%$ for classic rock/oldies, country, and top 40), and the prototypical distant-praise genre is the least consumed ($8.5\%$ for opera).

The partial points reveal how audiences for the same genre diverge by aspect. Like in our original MFA analysis focused on individuals, in the transposed MFA, each genre has three partial coordinates per dimension: one for the preference-audience (respondents who like it), one for the consumption-audience (respondents who listen), and one for the evaluation-audience (respondents who grant it high status). When these three points cluster together, a genre recruits the same people across all three aspects---likers and listeners and status-granters occupy the same region. When they spread far apart, a genre's audiences are segmented: the people who like it are positioned differently from those who listen to it or who value its fans highly. The configuration axis (Dimension 2 of Figure~\ref{fig:genre-map-d12}) shows this segmentation most starkly: certain genres (rap, reggae, metal) have their liking and listening audiences positioned on the negative pole but their evaluation audience positioned on the positive pole---meaning that people who grant these genres high status are a demographically and culturally distinct population from the people who actually like or listen to them. 

More broadly, three patterns emerge: opera stands alone with extreme segmentation across all dimensions---its status-granting audience is a separate population at every level of analysis. At the opposite end, classic rock and country show the strongest engagement-without-status pattern, where listeners are numerous but status-granters are scarce. Most other genres recruit relatively unified audiences where the same people like, listen, and evaluate, or where segmentation concentrates on a single dimension rather than cutting across multiple ways of relating to the music.

The fourth dimension captures how genres attract audiences whose status valuations diverge from their engagement patterns. The evaluation partial points of consecrated genres sit displaced toward positive values relative to their preference and consumption partial points (classical: $+2.3$ for evaluation against $+1.0$ for preference and $+0.9$ for consumption; opera: $+2.3$ against $-0.0$ and $+0.1$), while country shows the reverse displacement (evaluation $-0.8$ against $-3.1$ and $-4.1$). In substance, this dimension measures the \emph{status--engagement separation} at the genre level: prestige genres sit high not because their audiences like or listen more, but because status attributions extend to genres people rarely engage with, creating a population of evaluators distinct from the liking and listening audiences. Popular genres sit low, meaning their status-granting audiences are smaller or nonexistent relative to their liking audiences. This is the genre-level complement to the individual-level status-valuation dimension (Dimension 4 at the individual level): whereas respondents on that axis range from those who grant status to few genres to those who grant it to many, this genre-level dimension reveals which genres suffer the sharpest separation between who engages with them and who credits their fans with high status.

\centering

Black points: genre compromise positions; colored points: aspect partial points (segments connect each genre's compromise to its aspect-specific positions). The displacement of the evaluation partial points of classical music and opera, and the reverse displacement for country, show how status attributions segment audiences differently from liking and listening.}
\label{fig:genre-map-d14}

\section{Discussion}

This paper has pursued a geometric approach to measuring complex tastes---the misalignments between preference, consumption, and evaluation in cultural fields. The results support three core findings about musical taste in contemporary America.

\emph{First, the three aspects are empirically independent.} Preference and consumption correlate moderately (RV = 0.35), but evaluation is nearly orthogonal to both (RV = 0.01). This independence is the geometric signature of the complex-taste concept. If all three were measuring the same underlying thing, we could ignore two of them. But they don't. What you like, what you listen to, and what you praise are three separable judgments that follow different logics.

\emph{Second, the shared structure is primarily two-dimensional.} The first dimension is the classical highbrow--popular hierarchy. The second is volume: how many genres someone likes and listens to. Both dimensions are visible across all three aspects, reflecting shared cultural structures that shape how people organize musical taste. Evaluations are largely silent on these dimensions, appearing only modestly on the first and second, but dominating a distinct fourth dimension.

\emph{Third, complex tastes are ubiquitous.} The disagreement scores ($W_s$) account for $49\%$, $55\%$, $52\%$, and $66\%$ of variation on the four dimensions. Combinatorially, the average respondent holds $10.2$ of $20$ genres in complex configurations. Only 12 respondents (of 2,259) hold no complex configuration at all. This is not a marginal phenomenon. Complex tastes are woven throughout the taste landscape.

A surprising finding follows: complex tastes are not concentrated in any social group. Where respondents sit (whether they prefer highbrow or popular genres) is strongly predicted by age, education, and class. But how much their three aspects disagree is nearly unpredictable from demographics. The dispersion that makes a person's taste complex is orthogonal to the social positions that sort people by consumption patterns. This fits the individual-level theory. The independence of the aspects at the population level generates disagreement at the individual level whenever people don't occupy all three positions simultaneously.

Finally, the duality reveals something crucial: from the genre perspective, the aspects agree. Liking, listening, and evaluation audiences overlap substantially. But because individuals don't equally participate in all three audiences, complex tastes emerge. A person may be a genuine opera enthusiast (likes, listens, praises) or a genuinely uninterested person (none of the above) or any combination. The eight configurations are not rare types; they're how ordinary people relate to culture when three incompletely correlated judgment systems structure their engagement.

Future work might explore whether these patterns generalize to other cultural fields---visual art, film, fashion---or whether music has distinctive properties. The geometric approach makes possible precise measurement of the degree to which cultural judgment is unified or fragmented. The results here suggest it's fundamentally fragmented.

\section{Within-Configuration Variation in Disagreement Scores}
\label{app:config-variation}

Respondents classified into the same configuration type show substantial variation in their aspect-disagreement scores across all four dimensions. Figure~\ref{fig:config-variation} displays the mean and standard deviation of $W_s$ for each configuration, revealing that the overlap in disagreement levels both within and across configuration types explains why the correlation between the geometric and combinatorial measures is weak. This variation arises because the same configuration can manifest across different numbers of genres and with different internal structures: a respondent with one guilty pleasure genre will have very different W scores than one with many such genres, even though both respondents hold the same configuration type. The disagreement associated with a particular configuration depends not just on its presence, but on how spread out across the genre space it becomes.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig-config-variation} \caption{Aspect-disagreement scores by configuration type. Bars show the mean $W_s$ for each of Ma's eight configurations on each of the four dimensions; error bars show $\pm 1$ SD. The substantial overlap both within and across configuration types illustrates why configuration counts and geometric disagreement scores are only weakly correlated.}
\label{fig:config-variation}
\end{figure}

\section{The Combinatorial Measure: Ma's Eight Configurations}
\label{app:configurations}

The geometric measure locates complex tastes continuously in the common space. As a discrete complement, each genre--respondent pair can be classified into one of Ma's eight configurations from the binary triple of orientations (preference, consumption, evaluation): the simple taste $(+++)$, the simple non-taste $(---)$, and the six complex configurations.

Complex tastes are the statistical norm, not the exception \citep{ma2026deep-fb3}. Figure~\ref{fig:configurations} reports the mean number of genres held in each configuration: the average respondent holds $10.2$ of the $20$ genres in a complex configuration, and only $12$ of $2{,}259$ respondents hold no complex configuration at all. The most frequent complex configuration is the \emph{justified abstention} ($3.3$ genres on average), followed by the \emph{guilty pleasure} ($3.2$) and \emph{distant praise} ($2.2$): respondents routinely like genres whose fans they don't credit with high status, grant high status to genres they neither like nor consume, and like-and-consume genres whose fans they don't think of as high status. The taste pose ($1.0$) and the rare variants---distanced consumption ($0.4$) and the pre-acquired taste ($0.1$)---are comparatively infrequent, while the simple non-taste ($8.9$) is the single largest configuration.

\label{fig:configurations}
\end{figure}

\section{Genre-Specific Disagreement Across All Twenty Genres}
\label{app:omega-genres}

Figures~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d1}--\ref{fig:omega-genres-d4} extend the genre-by-demographic matrices of Figures~\ref{fig:omega-demographics-d1}--\ref{fig:omega-demographics-d4} to all twenty genres, one figure per dimension. Each cell reports the Pearson correlation between a demographic variable (columns) and the genre-based component $\omega_s(i;g)$ of the genre named in the row. All sixteen demographic variables are shown---the four own-education categories (high school or less, some college, bachelor's, postgraduate), parents' education, the four subjective-class identities (lower, working, middle, upper), age, gender, and the White, Black, Hispanic, Asian, and Multirace/Other category indicators. The encoding is as in Figures~\ref{fig:omega-demographics-d1}--\ref{fig:omega-demographics-d4}; blue cells are positive, red cells negative, and every value is printed.

The matrices confirm how localized the demographic patterning is. On the highbrow--popular dimension (Figure~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d1}) the age gradient dominates the popular block (rap/hip-hop $-0.44$, indie rock $-0.36$, heavy metal $-0.27$), the race indicators peak in Latin/salsa (Hispanic respondents $0.44$, White $-0.34$), and Black respondents show elevated disagreement in gospel ($0.25$) and blues ($0.23$). On the volume dimension (Figure~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d2}) the education contrasts appear (postgraduate respondents $0.17$ for opera and $0.15$ for musicals, parents' education $0.12$ for opera, classical music, and musicals) alongside the race contrasts in the diaspora genres (Hispanic respondents $0.34$ for Latin/salsa, Black respondents $0.20$ for gospel and $0.18$ for reggae). On the musical-family dimension (Figure~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d3}) the first dimension's age and race patterns recur at nearly full strength (rap/hip-hop $-0.44$; Latin/salsa $0.43$ for Hispanic respondents against $-0.34$ for White). On the status-valuation dimension (Figure~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d4}) the associations are weak throughout; the largest is postgraduate respondents in opera ($0.18$).
